title: The Moon Sings to the Boy
summary: Emilio doesn't want to go to sleep, because he says nothing happens when you sleep. The moon, watching him through the window, is going to show him otherwise.

scenes.text:
It was already night-time, but Emilio didn't want to go to sleep.

He tossed and turned. He kicked off the covers. He pulled them back on. He counted the squares on his quilt: blue, yellow, grey, blue.

"Sleeping is boring," he told the window. "You close your eyes, and nothing happens."

And the window answered him.

Well, not the window. The moon, who was peeping in right in the middle of it, thin and curved like a smile.

"Nothing happens?" said the moon, in a voice as soft as warm milk. "That's because you don't know how to look."

"Look with my eyes closed?"

"Try it. Close your eyes, and I'll sing you what's there."

Emilio closed his eyes.

The moon began to sing, very softly. It wasn't a song with words. It was more like a swing going back and forth.

And Emilio felt his bed begin to move. It rocked gently, from side to side.

His bed wasn't a bed any more. It was a boat. And all around the boat, blue and calm, there was a sea.

"A boat!" shouted Emilio, and he opened his eyes to see it.

But there was only his room. The chair. The wardrobe. The patchwork quilt.

"It's gone!" he complained.

"Of course it's gone," said the moon. "Dreams are shy. If you open your eyes, they hide."

Emilio closed his eyes again. This time, squeezed tight.

The moon kept on singing.

The boat came to the edge of a forest. But it wasn't any old forest. The trees were as tall as giraffes, and instead of leaves they had colourful kites, fluttering in the breeze.

Emilio walked among the trees. There was a swing hanging from a branch, so high it reached the clouds. There was a river of warm chocolate. There was a rabbit reading the newspaper, who turned a page and said goodnight to him.

Emilio really, really wanted to open his eyes, so he could go and tell Mum.

But he didn't open them.

"Now comes the best part," whispered the moon.

Emilio felt his body grow heavy. Heavy and warm, like when you climb into the bath.

And light, at the same time.

He breathed slowly. Once. Twice.

And he began to float. He rose above the forest of kites, above the clouds, among the stars, until he was very, very high up.

All the way to the moon.

The moon sat him in her curve, which was just the right size for a boy. And from there, Emilio saw the whole world asleep and silent, with all its windows dark.

"You see?" said the moon. "When you're asleep, lots and lots of things happen."

"Tomorrow I'll show you somewhere else," said the moon.

But Emilio didn't answer.

He was in his bed, with his quilt pulled up to his chin, hugging his little blue blanket. His mouth was a tiny bit open, and out of it came a teeny-tiny snore.

And the moon stayed at the window all night long, singing softly, watching over his dreams.

Just in case any of them wanted to hide.
